title: Birha: longing
hookLine: the ache of separation is honored in the Granth as part of love
last: SUHAGAN — THE SOUL IS A BRIDE.

cards: Think of an airport arrivals hall. People holding signs and flowers, craning at the sliding doors. Some have waited months.
Nobody would say they love less because they're waiting. If anything, the waiting is the love, made visible. Most of us treat missing someone, or missing God, as a problem to fix fast.
The Guru Granth Sahib doesn't hide that ache. It honors it, and gives it a name: birha.

teach.b: Birha is the pain of separation: the bride from the beloved, the soul from God. Yesterday's bride was united. Today's bride is at the window, still waiting, and the Granth gives her a lot of room.

Guru Arjan's Barah Maha walks through the twelve months of the year, and in month after month the bride aches for her beloved, in the heat, in the rains, in the cold. Guru Nanak has his own Barah Maha too.

The longing isn't treated as failure. It's a sign that love is alive. The boldest line comes from Sheikh Farid, a Sufi poet of the Punjab whose couplets the Gurus kept in the Granth; we'll meet him properly in two weeks.
In the original: birhaa birhaa aakheeai birhaa too sultaan.
People keep saying separation, separation; separation, you are the king. And then: the body in which this longing never rises, know it as a cremation ground. Strong words.
The ache, Farid says, is proof of life. A heart that never misses anything isn't peaceful. It's asleep.
Why honor pain? Because longing points.

teach.h: YOU ONLY MISS WHAT YOU LOVE.
teach.b: You can only miss what you love.
So in the Granth, birha is not the opposite of love. It's love, facing the door.
That's the week's thread too: the five thieves and nimrata, maya's passing pull, facing the Guru, the ease of sahaj, the soul as a bride, and now birha. Every one is about where the heart is facing.

how: Hymns of longing, including the Barah Maha of the twelve months, are sung in Sikh kirtan; many gurdwaras recite the Barah Maha in Majh on sangrand, the first day of each month in the Punjabi calendar.

o: the ache of being apart from the one you love
a song of the twelve months of the year
sadness that means your faith is failing

games.q: birha in the Granth — tap the pairs.
p: twelve months of the bride's longing

s: the Granth treats longing as a failure of faith
it honors the ache of separation as a sign that love is alive.
Sheikh Farid's couplets are part of the Guru Granth Sahib
the Gurus kept this Sufi poet's verses in the Granth.
Guru Arjan's Barah Maha moves through the twelve months of the year
month after month, the bride longs for her beloved.

games.q: you're aching for someone you can't reach. what does the Granth's picture of birha suggest?
o: treat the ache as a sign of love, and sit with it kindly.
games.why: Farid calls separation the king: a heart that never longs is asleep. you only miss what you love.

practice: Bring to mind one longing you carry: a person far away, someone who has died, a hope that hasn't come, or, if you pray, a longing for God.
Don't fix it or push it away; sit beside it kindly, the way you'd sit beside a friend in an arrivals hall. Breathe with it, and let it be what it is: a sign of love.

wordCard.voice: Birha. The ache of separation, honored in the Granth as part of love. This week's words: the five thieves, nimrata, maya, gurmukh, sahaj, suhagan, birha.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: birha, the pain of separation; Farid's salok calls it sultaan, the king.

carryVoice: Your line: longing is love too. A heart that misses is still awake. A full week, done.
